Yet it is established that it was by the soldiers, when they had said many things insultingly against him as against a boy, and against his mother as avaricious and greedy.

He reigned thirteen years and nine days. He lived twenty-nine years, three months, and seven days. He did everything by the counsel of his mother, with whom he was killed. The omens of his death were these. When he was celebrating his birthday, a bloodstained victim escaped and — since he bore himself courteously and was mingled with the people — stained his white robe, in which he had been standing. A huge and ancient laurel in the palace of a certain city, from which he was setting out to war, suddenly fell whole. Three fig trees, which bore those figs that are called Alexandrine, suddenly fell before his tent, when the imperial tents had been joined to them. A Druid woman cried out to him in the Gallic tongue, as he was going: "Go, but hope for no victory, nor trust yourself to your soldier." He mounted the tribunal to harangue and to say something auspicious, and began thus: "When the emperor Heliogabalus was killed." This too was an omen, that, about to go to war, he had begun to address the soldiers with a less auspicious speech.

But all these things he most vehemently despised, and, having set out to war in the place mentioned above, he was killed thus. He had lunched, as it happened, at a public banquet, as was his wont — that is, in open tents, taking soldier's food, for nothing else was found by the soldiers when they searched the tents; and while he was resting after the meal, about the seventh hour of the day, one of the Germans, who held the office of jester, having entered while all slept, was seen by the emperor alone, who was keeping awake. Alexander said to him: "What is this, comrade? Do you bring any news of the enemy?" But he, terrified with fear and hoping he could not escape, because he had burst into the prince's tent, came to his comrades and exhorted them to slay the strict prince. They, suddenly entering in numbers and armed, cut down the unarmed men who withstood them, and ran the emperor himself through with very many blows. Some say that nothing at all was said, but only that the soldiers cried out "Get out, withdraw," and so the excellent young man was cut down. But all the military equipment which was afterward led into Germany by Maximinus was Alexander's, and most powerful indeed, through Armenians and Osroeni and Parthians and men of every kind.

That Alexander despised death is declared both by that fierceness of mind by which he always wore down the soldier, and also by these things. Thrasybulus the mathematician was his most intimate friend. When he had told him that there was a necessity that he should perish by a barbarian sword, at first he rejoiced, because he believed a warlike and imperial death hung over him; then the man argued and showed that all the best men had been cut off by a violent death, saying that Alexander himself, whose name he bore, and Pompey, Caesar, Demosthenes, Tullius, and the rest of the famous men, had not met a quiet death. And he had so much spirit that he thought himself to be likened to the gods, if he should perish in war. But the matter deceived him; for he perished both by a barbarian sword and by the hand of a barbarian jester, yet not in war, but in time of war.

The soldiers, and those who had once been cashiered by him, bore his death most grievously and slew the authors of the slaughter. But the Roman people and all the senate, with all the provincials, took it neither more sadly nor more harshly ever — at the same time because the harshness and rusticity of his successor Maximinus, as a military man, to whom with his son the empire was offered after him, seemed to show a graver necessity of fate. The senate enrolled him among the gods; he won a cenotaph in Gaul, at Rome a most ample tomb. Sodal-priests too were appointed, who were called Alexandrini; and there were added festal days in his mother's name and his own, which are still today most religiously celebrated at Rome on his birthday. The cause of his being killed is reported by others to have been this: that his mother, the German war abandoned, wished to return to the East for her own ostentation, and on this account the army was angry. But these things were invented by the lovers of Maximinus, who did not wish it to seem that an excellent emperor had been killed by his own friend against human and divine law.

Up to this point the empire of the Roman people had this prince who ruled for a longer time; after him, when others rushed in upon one another in rivalry — some reigning six months, some a year, most for two years, at the most for three — down to those princes who extended the empire more widely, I mean Aurelian and thereafter. About these, if life supports me, we shall publish what shall be ascertained. These things were censured in Alexander: that he did not wish to be a Syrian; that he loved gold; that he was most suspicious; that he found out many taxes; that he wished to be thought a Great Alexander; that he was too severe toward the soldiers; that he conducted by private cares all the things which he had instituted in the state. I know indeed that very many deny that he was named Caesar by the senate, but by the soldiers — who are utterly ignorant of the truth; and they say besides that he was not the cousin of Heliogabalus. Let these, that they may follow us, read the historians of that time, and especially Acholius, who also wrote the itineraries of this prince.

You are wont to ask, most great Constantine, what it is that made a man a Syrian and of foreign birth so great a prince, when so many of the Roman race, so many of other provinces, are found base, impure, cruel, abject, unjust, lustful. First of all I can answer, from the opinion of good men, that it was possible by nature, which everywhere is one mother, that a good prince should be born; next, that by fear, because the worst had been killed, this man was made the best. But because the truth must be suggested, I shall unfold to your Clemency and Piety the things I have read. It is known to your Piety, what you have read in Marius Maximus, that a state is better and almost safer in which the prince is bad than one in which the prince's friends are bad; since one bad man can be corrected by very many good ones, but many bad men cannot by any reckoning be overcome by one, however good. And this indeed was said to Trajan himself by Homullus, when the latter said that Domitian had been most wicked but had had good friends, and therefore that man was the more to be hated who entrusted the state to men of worse life, because it is better to suffer one bad man than many.

But, to return to the matter, Alexander himself indeed was most excellent and used the counsels of a most excellent mother; and yet he had friends holy and venerable, not malicious, not thievish, not factious, not crafty, not consenting to evil, not enemies of the good, not lustful, not cruel, not deceivers of him, not mockers, not such as would lead him about as if a fool, but holy, venerable, continent, religious, loving their prince, and such as would neither themselves laugh at him nor wish him to be a laughing-stock; who sold nothing, lied in nothing, feigned nothing, never deceived the judgment of their prince but loved him. There is added to this that he had eunuchs neither in his counsels nor in his offices — they who alone ruin princes, while they wish them to live after the manner of nations or the kings of the Persians; who remove them from the people and from friends; who, being go-betweens, often report something other than is answered; who shut in their prince and contrive above all things that he should know nothing; who, since they have been bought and have been slaves, what good, after all, can they taste? In short, this was his own opinion: "I do not suffer chattels bought with bronze to judge concerning the heads of prefects and consuls and senators."

I know, emperor, that these things are said with danger before an emperor who has been a slave to such people; but, the state being safe — since you have understood what evil those pests hold and how they encompass princes — you too hold them in such a place that you have not even ordered them to use the cloak, but have delegated them to domestic necessities. There is besides that notable thing, that within the Palace he saw no one except the prefect and Ulpian indeed, nor gave anyone the opportunity either of selling smoke about himself or of speaking ill to him of others — especially after Turinus was killed, who had often sold him as if a fool and madman. There is added to this, that if Alexander found friends and kinsfolk bad, he either punished them, or, if old friendship or relationship did not allow them to be punished, dismissed them from him, saying: "The state is dearer to me than all these."

And that you may know what men were in his council: Fabius Sabinus, son of the distinguished Sabinus, the Cato of his time; Domitius Ulpianus, most skilled in law; Aelius Gordianus, parent of the emperor Gordian, a distinguished man; Julius Paulus, most skilled in law; Claudius Venacus, a most ample orator; Catilius Severus, his kinsman, the most learned man of all; Aelius Serenianus, the most holy man of all; Quintilius Marcellus, than whom not even the histories contain a better. By so many and other such men what evil could be thought or done, since they consented to the good? And these indeed the cohort of the wicked had driven off, which had encompassed Alexander in his first days; but by the young man's prudence, the wicked being slain and driven off, this holy friendship grew strong. These are they who made a good prince of a Syrian; and likewise the bad friends, who handed down even to posterity the worst Romans, labouring under their own vices.
